title: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde — Factual Accuracy Audit
novel: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

issues.lesson_title: Chapters 4–6: The Carew Murder and Incident at the Window
issues.claim: The broken walking stick belonged to Utterson — he had given it to Jekyll as a gift years earlier.
issues.correct: The cane belonged to Jekyll. Utterson had given it to Jekyll as a gift years before, so at the time of the murder it was Jekyll's property. The text reads: 'he recognised it for one that he had himself presented many years before to Henry Jekyll.' Hyde used Jekyll's cane, not Utterson's.
issues.source: Chapter 4 (The Carew Murder Case), Project Gutenberg text

issues.claim: Earlier Gothic novels like Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) and Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897) shared similar concerns about science overreaching its boundaries.
issues.correct: Dracula (1897) was published eleven years AFTER Jekyll and Hyde (1886), so it cannot be described as an 'earlier' Gothic novel. Frankenstein (1818) correctly predates Jekyll and Hyde. Dracula belongs to the same Gothic tradition but is a later work, not an earlier influence. The word 'Earlier' must be removed or Dracula repositioned as a contemporary/successor.
issues.source: Publication dates: Jekyll and Hyde 1886; Dracula 1897.

issues.claim: Eight months later, Hyde commits a far more terrible crime.
issues.correct: The text says 'Nearly a year later, in the month of October.' Eight months is too short; the novel specifies nearly a full year.
issues.source: Chapter 4 (The Carew Murder Case) opening sentence.

issues.claim: Lanyon describes his reaction: 'like a man restored from death.'
issues.correct: The phrase 'like a man restored from death' describes Jekyll's appearance to Lanyon, not Lanyon's reaction. The full text reads: 'pale and shaken, and half fainting, and groping before him with his hands, like a man restored from death — there stood Henry Jekyll!' The simile applies to how Jekyll looks, not to what Lanyon feels.
issues.source: Chapter 9 (Dr Lanyon's Narrative), Project Gutenberg text.

issues.claim: Utterson's clerk, Mr Guest, compares the handwriting to Jekyll's own and declares it a forgery.
issues.correct: Guest does not declare it a forgery. He says 'the two hands are in many points identical; only differently sloped.' It is Utterson who privately thinks 'Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer!' — an internal horror, not Guest's professional declaration. Guest observes a similarity; he makes no finding of forgery.
issues.source: Chapter 5 (Incident of the Letter), Project Gutenberg text.

issues.location: Chapter 4 Key Fact box — quote from novel
issues.claim: under which the bones were audibly shattering
issues.correct: The exact text is 'the bones were audibly shattered' (past passive). The lesson uses the present participle 'shattering' instead of the past participle 'shattered'. This is a misquotation of the original.
issues.source: Chapter 4 (The Carew Murder Case), Standard Ebooks / Project Gutenberg text.

issues.lesson_title: Chapters 4–6: The Carew Murder and Incident at the Window
issues.claim: Lesson is titled 'Chapters 4–6: The Carew Murder and Incident at the Window'
issues.correct: The 'Incident at the Window' is Chapter 7, not Chapter 6. This lesson covers Chapters 4 (Carew Murder), 5 (Letter) and 6 (Remarkable Incident of Dr Lanyon). The lesson content is accurate; only the title subtitle is wrong. AQA L4 (6cbead7a) correctly opens at Chapter 7.
issues.source: Chapter titles from Project Gutenberg: Chapter 6 = Incident of Dr Lanyon (or Remarkable Incident of Dr Lanyon); Chapter 7 = Incident at the Window.

issues.claim: Utterson is described as 'ausere with himself'
issues.correct: The word is 'austere', not 'ausere'. The Stevenson text reads 'He was austere with himself'. This is a typo/misquotation of a key word in a directly attributed quote.
issues.source: Chapter 1 (Story of the Door), Project Gutenberg text.

issues.claim: Jekyll describes his own impending death in present tense. 'This, then, is the last time… that Henry Jekyll can think his own thoughts or see his own face… in the glass.'
issues.correct: The phrase 'in the glass' is not in the original. The actual text reads: 'This, then, is the last time, short of a miracle, that Henry Jekyll can think his own thoughts or see his own face (now how sadly altered!) in the glass.' The phrase 'in the glass' IS in the original, but the ellipsis in the lesson omits 'short of a miracle' and 'now how sadly altered!' — making the quote appear artificially tidy. The lesson quotes the phrase as ending at 'in the glass' but the omission of 'short of a miracle' changes the nuance (Jekyll was not certain about the 'last time'). Minor but worth noting.
issues.source: Chapter 10 (Henry Jekyll's Full Statement), Project Gutenberg text.
issues.note: On re-reading, 'in the glass' IS in the original text — the issue is purely the omission of 'short of a miracle' which softens Jekyll's certainty. Downgraded to low.
